p.x:
Tomorrow is my English exam. I'm a bit nervous, but I'm ready. Today I read my notes again and checked my bag.
In my bag, I have two pencils, a rubber and a calculator for my maths test next week. My mum said, "Go to bed early!"
The exam has three parts. First, there is a listening test. Then we answer questions on the question paper. In the afternoon, there is a speaking test with a teacher. My teacher says, "Never leave an answer blank. Always guess!" My parents will take me to school in the morning. I hope I do well!

Almost every student feels stressed before an exam. You might get butterflies in your stomach or sweaty hands, and some people even panic and forget everything they know. A little pressure is normal and can help you focus, but too much can stop you from doing your best.
Good revision starts early. Instead of trying to cram everything the night before, make a plan for several weeks. Read your notes, use a highlighter to mark key ideas, and summarise each topic in a few sentences. Many students find that a mind map helps them see how ideas connect.
Practice is also important. Doing past papers shows you what kinds of questions to expect, and a mock exam lets you practise under real conditions. If your exam is multiple choice, learn to remove the wrong answers first. On the day, read the instructions carefully and fill in the answer sheet neatly. For an oral exam, practise speaking aloud and work on your pronunciation.
Finally, remember that one exam does not decide your whole life. If you don't pass, you can usually retake or resit it. Every year, many students achieve their goals on their second attempt. Learning a few coping strategies, such as deep breathing, can make a big difference.

In many East and Southeast Asian countries, exams play a central role in young people's lives. University entrance exams can determine not only which institution a student attends but also their future career and social status. Admission to the most prestigious universities is fiercely competitive, and students are often ranked nationally according to their scores.
To gain an advantage, millions of teenagers attend cram school in the evenings and at weekends, sometimes studying for twelve hours a day. The expectations of parents and teachers can be intense, and some students describe feeling that their entire worth depends on a single result. Schools themselves are under pressure, too, as they are compared in league tables based on exam performance.
Psychologists warn that this environment can encourage harmful patterns. A perfectionist may consider anything less than full marks a failure, while fear of failure can lead students to avoid challenges altogether. In the exam room, anxiety can have physical effects: a student's heart starts racing and their mind goes blank, even on topics they know well. Simply seeing the invigilator hand out papers can trigger panic.
Supporters of standardised tests argue that they are a fair and objective way to compare students from different backgrounds. Critics, however, believe they reward memorisation rather than creativity and fail to measure qualities such as teamwork and curiosity. Several countries are now experimenting with alternatives, including coursework and interviews.
